accuracy.evidence: Figures match Rohrer & Taylor 2007 (practice 89% blocked vs 60% mixed; one-week test 20% vs 63%), Taylor & Rohrer 2010 (77% vs 38%) and Kornell & Bjork 2008; the three area formulas and all six worked areas are correct.

misconceptions.evidence: Tackles judging by fluency, mixing unrelated topics, mixing a method before it is known, reading extra errors as failure, and confusing interleaving with spacing; challenge why() replies address each one.

lab_distinct.evidence: A practice-order lab: run blocked and mixed sessions, reveal the week-later bars, build a nine-chip set while a switch counter ticks, then pick area formulas for mixed shapes; unlike the forgetting-curve calendar in 449.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner sees blocked win in practice and then lose a week later before any rule is stated, then feels the choosing cost directly when mixed shapes force a formula decision each time.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions (which group wins in practice, which wins a week later, what to do with a brand-new method) are answered by the bars and the sort step; the trap options 'About the same' and 'Mix from the first question' are offered.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions; each wrong option has its own why() reply, e.g. 'Both groups did the same number of questions. Only the order changed' and '9 is the number of questions. Count the gaps where the type changes: 2'.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and a concrete triangle-trapezium example and passed the learner readability gate; adult paragraphs cite the studies with dates and define blocked, interleaved and spaced practice.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph defines a term, reports a study result, lists named mistakes or describes the lab; the family tip is a concrete instruction to shuffle revision question types and explains why it feels harder.

mobile.evidence: Android 360 px light and iPhone 13 dark screenshots show the session lanes, bars with labels below them, the nine-slot builder, readable formula cards and the sort bins; pool labels were split onto two lines to stop overlap.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas tap has a button twin (run sessions, test, add each type, clear, the three formulas, both sort bins), the canvas aria-label tracks feedback, and walk.cjs axe checks were clean in both themes.

sources: Rohrer, D. & Taylor, K. (2007). The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning. Instructional Science, 35, 481-498
Taylor, K. & Rohrer, D. (2010). The effects of interleaved practice. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 24, 837-848
Kornell, N. & Bjork, R. A. (2008). Learning concepts and categories: Is spacing the enemy of induction? Psychological Science, 19, 585-592
UK National Curriculum 2013, KS3 Mathematics: derive and apply formulae for the area of triangles, parallelograms and trapezia
